concepts.title: What a Summary Is and Is Not
concepts.definition: A summary restates the main points of a passage in fewer words, in the summariser's own language, as a connected paragraph meant for other readers. It is not a copying exercise, not a comment, and not as severely shortened as notes -- the full argument must survive in miniature.
concepts.key_idea: A summary is the passage shrunk, not shortened -- complete thought, fewer words, other people's eyes.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb112.txt opening (purpose of summarising, selection and compression, not as severely shortened as note making)
question_patterns: define summarising in your own words
in class 11 summarising: how does a summary differ from note making
why must a summary be written in third person
what is meant by selection and compression in a summary
should a summary include examples from the passage
what makes a summary useful to a reader who has not seen the original

solution_steps.explain: Identify the main points the passage exists to make; drop illustrations, repeats and digressions.
Re-express the selected points in fewer, connected words -- own phrasing, faithful meaning.
Write continuous prose in the third person so a stranger to the text can follow the argument.

concepts.title: Steps of Summarising
concepts.definition: Sound summarising follows steps: read the passage thoroughly; note or underline the main points; link them in logical order; draft the summary in one paragraph; count and trim to the prescribed length; and supply a suitable title if asked.
concepts.key_idea: Read, select, connect, compress, title -- five moves from passage to summary.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb112.txt steps sections (read carefully, note main points, rough draft, final draft, prescribed length, suitable title)
question_patterns: list the steps involved in summarising a passage
in class 11 summarising: why is a rough draft useful before the final summary
how is the prescribed length of a summary decided
when is a title needed for a summary
why must the summary follow the order of the original
summarise a given passage in about eighty words

solution_steps.explain: Full reading first, then marking the sentences that carry the argument's weight.
Join the marked points into one paragraph, then trim wording to meet the length limit.
A short title, drawn from the passage's central concern, completes the exercise.

concepts.title: Fidelity: Own Words, No New Ideas
concepts.definition: A summary must stay faithful: it adds no opinions, no new examples and no moralising of its own, and it reproduces the original's emphasis proportionately. own-words rendering checks real understanding -- if you cannot rephrase it, you have not grasped it.
concepts.key_idea: Faithful means proportional -- the summary's shape must mirror the passage's shape, with nothing added.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb112.txt fidelity sections (own words, no comments or new ideas, proportionate importance, check against original)
question_patterns: why should a summary contain no new ideas
in class 11 summarising: what does writing in your own words test
how is proportionate importance maintained in a summary
can a summary include the summariser's opinion
check a given summary against its passage for fidelity
what errors spoil the fidelity of a summary

solution_steps.explain: Keep the summariser's views, examples and conclusions out of the text entirely.
Give each main idea space proportional to its weight in the original.
Compare summary to passage point by point to confirm nothing is added, dropped or distorted.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Outline the procedure you would follow to summarise a 400-word passage in 80 words.

solution_template.explain: Read twice and underline the four or five sentences carrying the argument.
Link the underlined ideas in one paragraph, then cut words until about 80 remain.
Add a short title and verify no new idea or opinion has crept in.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student's summary of a passage on water conservation adds the sentence 'Everyone must stop using water for washing cars.' Is this acceptable? Why?

solution_template.explain: If the passage never made this specific demand, the sentence introduces a new idea.
Summaries may add nothing -- not even worthy advice.
Delete the sentence; keep only what the passage itself asserts.
